about: The tracker guide's spoken lines, one a stand (0 the welcome, 7 try it yourself): the robot speaks them. Rendered by node tools/studio/tracker-guide/voice.mjs (Kokoro-82M, af_heart, as tools/voice/README.md sets it up) into voice/NN.mp3; make.mjs then puts each into the scene as sounds/voice-NN.mp3. Written by the main conversation (25 November 2026); changed only where the app does otherwise (the builder's report lists each change).

lines.title: Welcome
lines.text: Hello. I'm the robot from the tutorial, and today I'm your stand-in. A tracker is a small puck that knows where it is in the room. Strap a few to your body, and a character can move as you move. Walk round the stands. Each one shows a way to wear them, from the fullest to the lightest.

lines.title: Eleven trackers
lines.text: This is the whole body, with eleven trackers. One on the front of the head. One on the front of the chest. One at the back of the hips, on the belt. One on the back of each hand. One on each upper arm, just above the elbow. One on each thigh, just above the knee. And one on top of each foot, at the front. With all eleven, nothing is guessed. Elbows and knees go exactly where yours go.

lines.title: The T-pose
lines.text: Before a character can follow you, we need to know which tracker is where. So the character stands in a T-pose, and you copy it. In a headset, you step into it, like stepping into a suit. Without one, it comes to you. Stand straight, arms out to the sides, and hold still for five seconds. Then we look at every device you have, a tracker, a controller, the headset, and tie each one to the bone it is nearest to. You see a line for every one. If a line looks wrong, you change it. Whatever has nothing tied to it, we work out. From then on, the character moves as you move.

lines.title: Six trackers
lines.text: You can leave five at home. Six still give us the whole body: head, hips, two hands, two feet. Now we work out the chest, the elbows and the knees for you. Elbows bend down and back, knees bend forward. It looks natural, but it is a guess.

lines.title: Feet and headset
lines.text: Lighter still. Wear a headset and hold its controllers. They already know where your head and your hands are. Add just two trackers, one on top of each foot. We work out your hips and everything in between. It is the quick way to get real footwork.

lines.title: Headset and controllers
lines.text: And with no trackers at all? A headset and two controllers still give us your head and your hands. The feet we make up. When you lean or walk, the character takes a step to keep up, one foot at a time. This is how you see other people in a shared room.

lines.title: Tracked hands
lines.text: Put the controllers down, and the headset can watch your bare hands instead. The body follows your wrists in the same way. Keep your hands where the headset can see them. Behind your back, it loses them.

lines.title: Try it yourself
lines.text: Now you. If trackers are switched on in this room, this robot is yours. Open this scene in the studio, turn on Edit, and select it. Put on whatever you have: trackers, a headset, controllers. Step into the robot, face the same way, and choose Line up with the performer. With only a headset, you can also switch on My body in the settings, and look down.
